subject: Mathematics
title: Designing the Garden Plot
hook: Raj and his grandmother plan a vegetable garden. Using perimeter and area, they calculate how much fence to buy and how much space they'll have to grow.

slides.title: Perimeter and Area
slides.storyContext: Summer vacation! Raj's grandmother wants to build a vegetable garden in the backyard. She asks Raj: 'How much fence do we need? And how much space will we have for vegetables?'

image.alt: Perimeter and Area — Perimeter and Area

slides.title: Measuring the Garden
slides.storyContext: Nani sketches a rectangular garden: 'The length is 8 meters and the width is 5 meters. We need to fence the edges and know how much soil to buy for the inside.'

image.alt: Measuring the Garden — Perimeter and Area

slides.title: What Is Perimeter?
slides.storyContext: Priya walks around the garden boundary, measuring: '5 meters, then 8 meters, then 5 meters, then 8 meters again.' Nani says: 'The total distance around is the perimeter!'

points.label: Perimeter
points.text: the total distance around the edge of a shape

points.label: Formula (rectangle)
points.text: Perimeter = 2 × length + 2 × width, or P = 2(l + w)

example.problem: A rectangular garden is 8 m long and 5 m wide. What's the perimeter?

slides.inSimpleWords: Perimeter is the distance around the outside of a shape.

image.alt: What Is Perimeter? — Perimeter and Area

slides.title: Raj's Garden Walk
slides.storyContext: Raj decides to walk around the garden plot to understand it better. He starts at one corner and walks along each side, counting his steps. 'I walked 8 steps down the length, then 5 steps across the width, then 8 steps back, then 5 steps to return.' Nani claps: 'You just found the perimeter by walking!'

points.text: Walking around the edge helps us see perimeter in action
Adding all sides gives the total distance around

slides.title: Perimeter Calculation Steps
slides.storyContext: Nani shows step-by-step: 'For an 8m × 5m rectangle, add all four sides: 8 + 5 + 8 + 5.'

example.problem: Calculate perimeter by adding individual sides: 8 + 5 + 8 + 5
example.solution: 8 + 5 + 8 + 5 = 26 meters. Or using formula: 2(8 + 5) = 26 meters

slides.inSimpleWords: You can add each side individually or use the shortcut formula.

slides.title: Perimeter of Different Shapes
slides.storyContext: Raj suggests: 'What if the garden were square? Or triangular?' Nani explains the formulas for each shape.

points.label: Square
points.text: Perimeter = 4 × side (all 4 sides are equal)

points.label: Triangle
points.text: Perimeter = side₁ + side₂ + side₃ (add all 3 sides)

points.label: Circle
points.text: Perimeter (circumference) = 2πr or πd (π ≈ 3.14)

example.problem: A square garden has sides of 6 meters. What's the perimeter?
example.solution: P = 4 × 6 = 24 meters

slides.inSimpleWords: Each shape has its own perimeter formula—add up all the sides.

image.alt: Perimeter of Different Shapes — Perimeter and Area

slides.title: Perimeter Story: Triangular Corner
slides.storyContext: Priya suggests: 'What if we add a triangular storage corner with sides 3 m, 3 m, and 4 m?'

example.problem: Find the perimeter of a triangle with sides 3 m, 3 m, and 4 m
example.solution: P = 3 + 3 + 4 = 10 meters

slides.inSimpleWords: Just add up all three sides to find the triangle's perimeter.

slides.title: Real Fence at the Store
slides.storyContext: Raj visits the hardware store with Nani. The shopkeeper asks: 'How much fencing do you need?' Raj confidently says: '26 meters for the rectangle.' The shopkeeper approves and starts measuring out the fence. 'Good math, young man!'

points.text: Perimeter calculations solve real problems
Shopkeepers use geometry daily

slides.title: What Is Area?
slides.storyContext: Now Raj measures the inside: 'How much space is inside for planting?' Nani replies: 'That's the area—the space covered by a shape.'

points.label: Area
points.text: the space covered inside a flat shape, measured in square units

points.label: Square meter (m²)
points.text: a square with sides of 1 meter

example.problem: What does '8 square meters' mean?
example.solution: An area that can be covered by 8 squares of 1 meter × 1 meter

slides.inSimpleWords: Area is how much flat surface something covers.

slides.title: Counting Square Units
slides.storyContext: Raj imagines dividing the garden into 1-meter squares. 'If I count all the little squares, that's the area!' He counts 8 rows of 5 squares: 40 squares total. Nani smiles: 'Yes, Raj! That's exactly how area works.'

points.text: Area can be found by counting square units inside a shape
The 8-by-5 grid gives us 40 square meters

slides.title: Area of Rectangles and Squares
slides.storyContext: Raj counts small squares: 'If the garden is 8 meters long and 5 meters wide, I can fit 8 × 5 = 40 unit squares inside!'

points.label: Rectangle area
points.text: Area = length × width

points.label: Square area
points.text: Area = side × side (or side²)

example.problem: Raj's 8 m × 5 m garden has what area?
example.solution: Area = 8 × 5 = 40 square meters (m²)

slides.inSimpleWords: For a rectangle, just multiply length times width.

image.alt: Area of Rectangles and Squares — Perimeter and Area

slides.title: Square Garden Example
slides.storyContext: Priya finds a square plot nearby. 'This plot is 6 meters on each side. How much area does it have?'

example.problem: A square garden has sides of 6 meters. What's its area?
example.solution: Area = 6 × 6 = 36 square meters (m²)

slides.inSimpleWords: For a square, multiply side × side.

slides.title: Area of Triangles
slides.storyContext: Priya sketches a triangular garden corner: 'How do we find area of a triangle?' Nani explains: 'A triangle is half a rectangle!'

points.label: Triangle area
points.text: Area = (base × height) ÷ 2, or A = ½ × b × h

points.label: Tip
points.text: Height is perpendicular (straight up) from the base

example.problem: A triangle has base 6 m and height 4 m. What's its area?
example.solution: Area = (6 × 4) ÷ 2 = 24 ÷ 2 = 12 square meters

slides.inSimpleWords: Triangle area is half of base times height.

image.alt: Area of Triangles — Perimeter and Area

slides.title: The Rectangle and Triangle Connection
slides.storyContext: Nani draws a rectangle and then divides it diagonally. 'See? Two triangles fit inside. So each triangle is half the rectangle.' Raj has an 'aha' moment: 'That's why we divide by 2!'

points.text: Two identical triangles make one rectangle
Triangle area is half of rectangle area

slides.title: Combining Shapes: Rectangle + Triangle
slides.storyContext: Nani proposes a garden design: '8 m × 5 m rectangle for vegetables, plus a triangular corner (base 3 m, height 2 m) for storage.'

example.problem: Calculate total area for rectangle 8m×5m and triangle base 3m height 2m
example.solution: Rectangle: 8 × 5 = 40 m². Triangle: (3 × 2) ÷ 2 = 3 m². Total: 40 + 3 = 43 m²

slides.inSimpleWords: Add areas of individual shapes to get the total.

slides.title: Planning the Full Garden
slides.storyContext: Nani finalizes the plan: 'An 8 m × 5 m rectangular garden with a triangular storage corner (base 3 m, height 2 m).'

example.problem: Find perimeter and area for: rectangle 8m×5m + triangle base 3m height 2m. How much fence and soil?
example.solution: Rectangle perimeter: 2(8+5) = 26 m. Rectangle area: 40 m². Triangle area: 12 m². Total area for planting: 40 + 12 = 52 m² (but fence is just rectangle = 26 m)

slides.inSimpleWords: Perimeter tells you fence needed; area tells you soil needed.

slides.title: Shopping for Supplies
slides.storyContext: Raj and Nani head to the garden store. 'We need 26 meters of fencing,' Raj tells the shopkeeper. 'And we need soil for 40 square meters!' The shopkeeper confirms their quantities. Priya laughs: 'Math works in real life!'

points.text: Perimeter tells us how much fencing to buy
Area tells us how much soil to purchase

slides.title: Planting Day
slides.storyContext: A week later, the garden is built and fenced. Raj plants tomatoes, peppers, and cucumbers in the 40 m² area. 'The fence kept animals out,' he notes. 'And the soil fills exactly the space inside!' Nani hugs him: 'You designed this perfectly with math!'

points.text: Good math planning makes construction efficient
No waste, no shortage, perfect fit

slides.title: Learning Applied
slides.storyContext: Weeks later, the garden thrives. Nani tells Raj: 'Your mathematical thinking designed this entire garden. Perimeter protected our plants. Area gave us space to grow!' Raj realizes math isn't just numbers—it's real.

points.text: Math is everywhere in daily life
Good planning leads to successful outcomes

slides.title: Your Turn to Design
slides.storyContext: Design a garden: rectangular section 6 m × 4 m for vegetables, triangular section base 5 m height 3 m for herbs. Calculate total perimeter and area needed.

example.problem: Find fence needed and soil needed for: 6m×4m rectangle + 5m base × 3m height triangle
example.solution: Rectangle perimeter: 2(6+4)=20m. Rectangle area: 24m². Triangle area: (5×3)÷2=7.5m². Total area: 31.5m². Fence: 20m + sides of triangle

slides.inSimpleWords: Plan real gardens or rooms using perimeter and area formulas!

image.alt: Your Turn to Design — Perimeter and Area

slides.title: Challenge: Room Flooring
slides.storyContext: Raj's room is rectangular, 4 m long and 3 m wide. His parents want to tile the floor. How much tiling material do they need? Also, they want to add a border trim around the room edges.

example.problem: Room: 4 m × 3 m. How much tiling for the floor? How much trim for the border?
example.solution: Floor area: 4 × 3 = 12 m². Trim (perimeter): 2(4 + 3) = 14 m.

slides.inSimpleWords: Area tells you how much to cover the floor; perimeter tells you how much trim for the edges.

slides.title: Challenge: Comparing Shapes
slides.storyContext: Priya asks: 'If two gardens have the same perimeter but different shapes, do they always have the same area?' Let's find out with examples.

example.problem: Garden A: 6m×4m. Garden B: 7m×3m. Both have perimeter 20m. Which has more area?
example.solution: A: Area = 6×4 = 24 m². B: Area = 7×3 = 21 m². Same perimeter (20m) but Garden A has more area. Squares are most efficient!

slides.inSimpleWords: Perimeter and area are independent—shapes can have same perimeter but different areas.

slides.title: Challenge: L-Shaped Garden
slides.storyContext: Nani shows an L-shaped garden plot. 'Can you find its area?' Raj realizes he can split it into two rectangles.

example.problem: An L-shaped garden: top rectangle 6m×2m, bottom rectangle 4m×3m (overlapping 2m×1m). Find total area.
example.solution: Area = (6×2) + (4×3) - (2×1) = 12 + 12 - 2 = 22 m². Or split differently: 6×2 = 12, plus 4×2 = 8, plus 2×1 = 2. Total = 22 m²

slides.inSimpleWords: Complex shapes can be split into simpler rectangles.

points.text: Perimeter is the distance around the edge of a shape
Rectangle perimeter: 2(length + width)
Area is the flat space inside a shape (in square units)
Rectangle area: length × width
Triangle area: (base × height) ÷ 2
Use perimeter for fencing, area for covering materials

image.alt: What You've Learned — Perimeter and Area

subject: Mathematics
title: Building with Compass and Straightedge
hook: Raj learns to draw perfect geometric shapes using only a compass and straightedge, discovering the art and precision of construction.

slides.title: Playing with Constructions
slides.storyContext: In geometry class, Ms. Sharma challenges Raj and Priya: 'Can you draw a perfect circle? A perfect square? Using ONLY a compass and straightedge?'

image.alt: Playing with Constructions — Playing with Constructions

slides.title: The Challenge
slides.storyContext: Ms. Sharma hands out compass and straightedge tools: 'Forget rulers with numbers. In ancient geometry, we used only these two tools. Can you construct perfect shapes?' Raj's eyes light up: 'A puzzle to solve!'

image.alt: The Challenge — Playing with Constructions

slides.title: Tools of Construction
slides.storyContext: Ms. Sharma explains: 'A compass draws perfect circles. A straightedge draws perfectly straight lines. That's all we need!'

points.label: Compass
points.text: draws circles and arcs; keeps a fixed distance

points.label: Straightedge
points.text: draws perfectly straight lines; no measurements or marks

points.label: Tip
points.text: These tools can't measure—you use them to copy distances

slides.inSimpleWords: A compass is for circles, a straightedge is for straight lines.

image.alt: Tools of Construction — Playing with Constructions

slides.title: Priya's First Circle
slides.storyContext: Priya takes the compass nervously. 'Do I just... put it on paper and turn it?' Ms. Sharma nods. Priya carefully places one leg on the paper and spins the compass. A perfect circle appears! 'It worked!' she squeals.

points.text: A compass has two legs: a needle and a pencil
One leg stays fixed at the center, the other draws the circle

slides.title: Constructing a Circle
slides.storyContext: Priya tries: 'I just need to fix the compass legs and swing it around!' She produces a perfect circle.

points.label: Given
points.text: a point (center) and a distance (radius)

points.label: Steps
points.text: 1. Mark the center point. 2. Set compass to the radius distance. 3. Place one leg on center, swing the other leg around.

example.problem: Draw a circle with center O and radius 3 cm
example.solution: Mark O. Set compass to 3 cm. Place needle on O, draw the circle by rotating

slides.inSimpleWords: Fix one compass point at the center, swing the other to trace the circle.

image.alt: Constructing a Circle — Playing with Constructions

slides.title: Radius vs. Diameter
slides.storyContext: Ms. Sharma asks: 'If you set your compass to 3 cm and draw a circle, what's the diameter?' Raj thinks: 'The diameter is across the whole circle, so 2 × 3 = 6 cm!'

points.text: Radius is the distance from center to edge
Diameter is twice the radius

slides.title: Constructing Equal Line Segments
slides.storyContext: Ms. Sharma gives Raj a task: 'This line segment is 4 cm. Copy it exactly using the compass!'

points.label: Steps
points.text: 1. Set compass to the length of the segment. 2. Mark a new point. 3. Without changing compass, place needle on new point and mark the endpoint.

points.label: Result
points.text: Two segments of exactly equal length

example.problem: Given segment AB, construct an equal segment CD
example.solution: Set compass to AB length. Mark point C. Place compass needle on C, swing to mark D. CD = AB

slides.inSimpleWords: Use compass to copy a segment's length without measuring it.

image.alt: Constructing Equal Line Segments — Playing with Constructions

slides.title: Copying Without Measuring
slides.storyContext: Raj succeeds in copying a line segment. Ms. Sharma asks: 'Did you measure? Did you use a ruler?' Raj shakes his head. 'No! The compass just remembered the length and copied it!' Ms. Sharma smiles. 'Exactly. The compass stores distance in its opening.'

points.text: The compass opening holds a measurement
You can copy that distance to another location

slides.title: Constructing Perpendicular Lines
slides.storyContext: Priya asks: 'How do I make a right angle?' Ms. Sharma shows: 'Use compass arcs on both sides of a line, then connect the arcs. It creates 90 degrees!'

points.label: Given
points.text: a line and a point on it

points.label: Steps
points.text: 1. From point, mark equal arcs on both sides. 2. From each arc, draw arcs above/below that intersect. 3. Connect intersection to point. This is perpendicular!

points.label: Result
points.text: A 90-degree angle

slides.inSimpleWords: Perpendicular lines meet at exactly 90 degrees, forming a right angle.

image.alt: Constructing Perpendicular Lines — Playing with Constructions

slides.title: The Arcs Form a Cross
slides.storyContext: As Priya draws her intersecting arcs, a cross-like pattern emerges on her paper. Ms. Sharma points: 'Those arcs are equidistant. Where they cross is exactly 90 degrees from your original line.'

points.text: Perpendicular means 'standing straight up' from a line
Right angles are fundamental in geometry

slides.title: Constructing an Equilateral Triangle
slides.storyContext: Raj attempts: 'Can I make a triangle with all three sides equal?' Ms. Sharma guides: 'Yes! Draw a segment, then use compass to find the third vertex!'

points.label: Given
points.text: two points A and B (one side of the triangle)

points.label: Steps
points.text: 1. Set compass to AB length. 2. From A, draw an arc above. 3. From B, draw an arc above. 4. Mark intersection as C. 5. Connect A-C and B-C.

points.label: Result
points.text: Triangle ABC with all three sides equal

example.problem: Construct an equilateral triangle with side 3 cm
example.solution: Mark A and B 3 cm apart. Set compass to 3 cm. Swing from A and B above. Connect intersections. All three sides equal 3 cm

slides.inSimpleWords: Three equal sides means all three corners look the same.

image.alt: Constructing an Equilateral Triangle — Playing with Constructions

slides.title: Where the Arcs Meet
slides.storyContext: Raj draws two large arcs from points A and B. 'Where they cross... that's my third point!' he says excitedly. Ms. Sharma confirms: 'Yes. And because each arc has the same radius as AB, all three sides will be equal.'

points.text: The intersection of two arcs creates the third vertex
All three sides are equal to the compass opening

slides.title: Triangle Angles
slides.storyContext: Ms. Sharma points out: 'In an equilateral triangle, all three angles are equal—60 degrees each! 60 + 60 + 60 = 180.'

example.problem: What are the angles in an equilateral triangle?
example.solution: All three angles are 60°. Total: 60° + 60° + 60° = 180°

slides.inSimpleWords: Equal sides create equal angles.

slides.title: Constructing a Square
slides.storyContext: Ms. Sharma challenges: 'A square has four equal sides and four right angles. Build one using compass and straightedge!'

points.label: Steps
points.text: 1. Draw segment AB. 2. Construct perpendicular line at A. 3. Mark equal distance on perpendicular (point D). 4. From D, construct perpendicular. 5. Mark equal distance (point C). 6. Connect all corners.

points.label: Result
points.text: A perfect square with four equal sides and four right angles

slides.inSimpleWords: Construct two perpendiculars at the right angles, make sides equal with compass.

image.alt: Constructing a Square — Playing with Constructions

slides.title: Priya's Square Success
slides.storyContext: Priya carefully constructs a square by combining perpendiculars and equal segments. When she finishes, Ms. Sharma measures all sides and angles. 'Perfect! Four equal sides, four right angles. You've built a geometric masterpiece!'

points.text: Combining construction techniques creates more complex shapes
Accuracy requires careful, deliberate steps

slides.title: Constructing an Angle Bisector
slides.storyContext: Priya sketches an angle: 'Can I split this angle exactly in half?' Ms. Sharma shows the compass method.

example.problem: Given angle ABC, construct a line that divides it into two equal parts
example.solution: 1. From B (vertex), draw equal arcs intersecting both sides. 2. From both intersection points, draw equal arcs that meet. 3. Connect B to this meeting point. This bisects the angle

slides.inSimpleWords: Use compass arcs to find the exact middle of any angle.

image.alt: Constructing an Angle Bisector — Playing with Constructions

slides.title: Splitting an Angle
slides.storyContext: Raj draws a large angle and asks Ms. Sharma: 'Can we make it into two smaller equal angles?' She guides him through the arc method. His bisector line divides the angle perfectly in half!

points.text: Bisecting means splitting into two equal parts
Arc intersections find the exact dividing line

slides.title: Bisecting a 90° Angle
slides.storyContext: Ms. Sharma gives them a right angle to bisect. 'Split this 90° into two 45° angles using only compass arcs.'

example.problem: Bisect a 90-degree right angle to create two 45-degree angles
example.solution: From vertex B, draw equal arcs cutting both sides of the right angle. From those arc endpoints, draw equal arcs that meet. Connect B to this meeting point. Result: two 45° angles

slides.inSimpleWords: The bisector of a 90° angle creates two 45° angles.

slides.title: Build Your Own Construction
slides.storyContext: Ms. Sharma gives final challenge: 'Using compass and straightedge, construct a square. Then bisect one of its angles. Show me the steps!'

example.problem: Construct a square with side 4 cm, then bisect one of its 90° angles
example.solution: Square: AB=4cm, perpendicular at A and B, mark 4cm on perpendiculars to get C and D, connect CD. Bisect corner angle: from vertex, swing equal arcs, from arc intersections swing meeting arcs, connect to vertex. This creates two 45° angles

slides.inSimpleWords: Master compass construction by combining these techniques!

image.alt: Build Your Own Construction — Playing with Constructions

slides.title: Challenge: Construct a Hexagon Base
slides.storyContext: Ms. Sharma challenges: 'Start with an equilateral triangle. Can you construct a second triangle below it (inverted) using the same compass opening to create a larger shape?'

example.problem: Construct two equilateral triangles side-by-side with the same side length
example.solution: First triangle: set compass to 3 cm, draw arc intersections above. Second triangle: use the same compass opening on a parallel base, draw arc intersections below. Both share equal sides.

slides.inSimpleWords: Combining equal triangles creates more complex patterns.

slides.title: Challenge: Midpoint Construction
slides.storyContext: Ms. Sharma gives one more challenge: 'Given a line segment, find its exact midpoint using only compass and straightedge. No measuring allowed!'

example.problem: Find the exact midpoint of segment AB using compass construction
example.solution: Set compass wider than half of AB. From A, draw an arc above and below. From B, draw equal arcs. Connect the two intersection points. This perpendicular bisector crosses AB at its exact midpoint.

slides.inSimpleWords: A perpendicular bisector finds the midpoint and creates a right angle at once.

slides.title: Challenge: Regular Pentagon
slides.storyContext: Ms. Sharma asks: 'Can you construct a regular pentagon (5 equal sides, 5 equal angles)?' Raj scratches his head—this is very complex but possible with compass and straightedge.

example.problem: Construct a regular pentagon with compass and straightedge (advanced)
example.solution: This requires multiple steps: construct a circle, mark 5 equal arc positions (72° each), connect them. Each interior angle is 108°. This is an advanced construction!

slides.inSimpleWords: Regular pentagons need careful arc placements around a circle.

points.text: A compass and straightedge are tools for perfect geometric construction
Compass can draw circles and copy distances exactly
Straightedge draws perfectly straight lines without measuring
Use compass arcs to construct perpendiculars and angle bisectors
Equilateral triangles have three equal sides and 60° angles
Squares have four equal sides and four 90° right angles

image.alt: What You've Learned — Playing with Constructions

subject: Mathematics
title: Meera's Mirror Quest
hook: Discover how nature mirrors perfection — from butterflies to rangoli.

characters.name: Ravi
characters.role: Meera's friend who spots patterns everywhere

slides.title: The Morning Discovery
slides.storyContext: Meera wakes up and sees a butterfly landing on her window. She notices that one wing looks exactly like the other, just flipped. Her grandfather Dada is drawing a beautiful rangoli (floor art made with coloured powder) in the courtyard. Meera runs down to watch. She asks Dada why his rangoli is so perfectly balanced. Dada smiles and says: 'Beta, nature teaches us about symmetry. Come, let's explore it together with your friend Ravi.'

image.alt: The Morning Discovery — Symmetry

slides.title: What is a Line of Symmetry?
slides.storyContext: Dada folds his drawing of a flower in half. Both halves match perfectly. He tells Meera: 'This fold line is the line of symmetry. If you fold paper along this line, both sides fit exactly.'

points.label: Definition
points.text: A line of symmetry divides a shape into two identical halves that match perfectly when folded.

points.label: Test
points.text: Fold along the line — if both sides match, it is a line of symmetry.

example.problem: A heart shape has a vertical line drawn down its middle. When you fold the paper along this line, do the two halves match?
example.solution: Yes, the left half and right half are identical mirror images. This is a line of symmetry.

slides.inSimpleWords: A line of symmetry is an imaginary line where one side of a shape is a perfect mirror image of the other side.

image.alt: What is a Line of Symmetry? — Symmetry

slides.title: Meera's Folding Experiment
slides.storyContext: Meera takes colored paper and cuts out a butterfly shape. She folds it along the center. 'Look Dada! Both wings match!' Dada nods approvingly. 'That's the line of symmetry working. Nature designed butterflies this way for balance.'

points.text: The fold test is the easiest way to find symmetry
Matching halves indicate a line of symmetry

slides.title: Vertical and Horizontal Lines of Symmetry
slides.storyContext: Ravi brings an old door key from his house. He shows it to Meera. 'Look! If I draw a line down the middle, both sides match.' Then Dada draws a bridge on paper. 'This bridge has a horizontal line of symmetry — see how the top and bottom are the same?'

points.label: Vertical Line
points.text: Goes up and down. Splits the shape so left and right sides are identical.

points.label: Horizontal Line
points.text: Goes left and right. Splits the shape so top and bottom are identical.

example.problem: The letter 'A' is drawn on paper. Does it have a vertical line of symmetry?
example.solution: Yes. If you draw a line down the middle of 'A', the left half and right half match exactly.

slides.inSimpleWords: Vertical symmetry splits left and right; horizontal symmetry splits top and bottom.

slides.title: Testing Different Directions
slides.storyContext: Ravi experiments: 'What if I fold the letter 'A' sideways?' The halves don't match. 'Only works vertically!' he announces. Meera adds: 'So the direction of the line matters!'

points.text: Different shapes have symmetry in different directions
Testing all directions helps find all lines of symmetry

slides.title: Diagonal Symmetry
slides.storyContext: Dada draws a square. 'Watch! This square has symmetry along the diagonal too!' He draws from corner to corner and folds. 'Both triangles match!'

example.problem: Does a square have diagonal lines of symmetry?
example.solution: Yes! A square has 2 diagonal lines of symmetry, one from each pair of opposite corners. A rectangle does NOT have diagonal symmetry.

slides.inSimpleWords: Squares have symmetry in 4 directions: vertical, horizontal, and 2 diagonals.

slides.title: Symmetry in Indian Designs
slides.storyContext: Dada shows Meera a photograph of a traditional rangoli from the Diwali celebration. 'Every part has perfect balance. This is how we create beauty in our Indian art.' He also points to a kolam design (from South India) in a magazine. 'Look, multiple lines of symmetry!'

points.label: Rangoli
points.text: Traditional floor art with 1 or more lines of symmetry.

points.label: Multiple Symmetries
points.text: Some shapes have 2, 3, 4, or more lines of symmetry.

points.label: Real Example
points.text: A square has 4 lines of symmetry: 2 vertical/horizontal through midpoints, 2 diagonal through corners.

example.problem: How many lines of symmetry does a rectangle have?
example.solution: A rectangle has 2 lines of symmetry: one vertical through the middle and one horizontal through the middle. The diagonals do NOT create symmetry for a rectangle.

slides.inSimpleWords: Indian rangoli and kolam designs use symmetry to create beautiful, balanced patterns.

slides.title: Rangoli Symmetry Lesson
slides.storyContext: Dada draws a simple rangoli and explains: 'I draw one quarter, then mirror it three more times. Symmetry ensures it's perfectly balanced every time.' Meera watches as he creates a stunning diamond pattern.

points.text: Artists use symmetry to speed up their work
Mirroring patterns creates professional results

slides.title: Rotational Symmetry
slides.storyContext: Ravi spins a plate (thali) at home. 'Meera! When I spin it, it looks the same from every angle!' Meera realizes: 'That's different from folding. This is rotation!' Dada nods. 'Yes, beta. This is rotational symmetry — a shape looks the same after you turn it.'

points.label: Definition
points.text: Rotational symmetry means a shape looks identical after turning it by a certain angle.

points.label: Order
points.text: The number of times a shape matches as you rotate it 360° is its order of rotational symmetry.

points.label: Example
points.text: A square has rotational symmetry of order 4: it looks the same after turning 90°, 180°, 270°, and 360°.

example.problem: A plus sign (+) is rotated 90° clockwise. Does it look the same?
example.solution: Yes. A plus sign looks identical after rotating 90°. Its rotational symmetry has order 4 (matches at 90°, 180°, 270°, 360°).

slides.inSimpleWords: Rotational symmetry is when a shape looks the same after you spin it around.

slides.title: Spinning the Thali
slides.storyContext: Meera carefully spins the plate and marks its position. She rotates it 90 degrees. 'It looks the same!' She continues at 180°, 270°, and 360°. Dada explains: 'Every 90 degrees, the plate returns to an identical position. That's order-4 rotational symmetry.'

points.text: Some shapes match at regular angle intervals
The 'order' counts how many matching positions exist

slides.title: Symmetry in Nature and Everyday Life
slides.storyContext: Meera and Ravi take a walk in the garden. They see: a butterfly with matching wings, a leaf with veins on both sides, a sunflower with repeating petals, a ladybug with spots arranged symmetrically. Meera says: 'Symmetry is everywhere!' Dada adds: 'And in our homes too — doors, windows, tiles on the floor.'

points.label: Living Things
points.text: Butterflies, leaves, flowers, animals have symmetry for balance and beauty.

points.label: Man-Made
points.text: Buildings, doors, windows, tiles, and vehicles use symmetry in design.

points.label: Cultural
points.text: Indian textiles, jewelry, and architecture all use symmetry.

example.problem: A ceramic tile shows a peacock design. The peacock's body has vertical symmetry. If one eye is drawn, and the tile is folded vertically, where should the other eye appear?
example.solution: On the opposite side of the vertical line, in the exact same position relative to the center. This is a mirror image.

slides.inSimpleWords: Symmetry appears in nature (animals, plants) and in things we design and build.

slides.title: Finding Symmetry Everywhere
slides.storyContext: Ravi spots a peacock feather: 'Look at the eye on the feather!' Meera sees vertical symmetry in the pattern. They find symmetry in leaves, in door handles, in window designs. Dada concludes: 'Nature and humans both love balance and symmetry.'

points.text: Symmetry is both a natural principle and a design choice
Learning to spot symmetry trains your observation skills

slides.title: Worked Problem: Finding All Lines of Symmetry
slides.storyContext: Dada gives Meera a challenge. 'Draw a rectangle and find all its lines of symmetry. I'll give you a hint: fold it different ways and see which folds give you matching halves.'

example.problem: A rectangle has length 10 cm and width 6 cm. Meera wants to find all lines of symmetry. List them.
example.solution: A rectangle has 2 lines of symmetry: (1) A vertical line passing through the center, dividing left and right halves equally. (2) A horizontal line passing through the center, dividing top and bottom halves equally. Note: The diagonals do NOT produce symmetry in a rectangle (they only do in a square).

slides.inSimpleWords: A rectangle has 2 lines of symmetry, one vertical and one horizontal through the center.

slides.title: Rectangle vs. Square
slides.storyContext: Meera asks: 'Does a square have more symmetry than a rectangle?' Dada draws both shapes. 'A square has 4 lines of symmetry including diagonals. A rectangle has only 2, just vertical and horizontal. Why? Because a square's sides are all equal!'

points.text: Equal sides create additional diagonal symmetries
More symmetry requires perfect equality in all dimensions

slides.title: Symmetry in Indian Letters
slides.storyContext: Ravi brings a Hindi book. 'Look! The letter क (ka) has vertical symmetry!' Meera examines others: 'And म (ma) too!' They realize Indian scripts have beautiful symmetric forms, making them easier to write and recognize.

points.text: Script design uses symmetry for clarity
Cultural mathematics shows up everywhere

slides.title: Symmetry Orders of Shapes
slides.storyContext: Dada asks: 'What's the rotational symmetry order of: a triangle, a square, a hexagon?'

example.problem: Find the rotational symmetry order for: (A) equilateral triangle, (B) square, (C) regular hexagon
example.solution: (A) Equilateral triangle: order 3 (matches at 120°, 240°, 360°). (B) Square: order 4 (matches at 90°, 180°, 270°, 360°). (C) Regular hexagon: order 6 (matches at 60°, 120°, 180°, 240°, 300°, 360°)

slides.inSimpleWords: More sides mean more rotational symmetry positions.

slides.title: Your Turn: Spot the Symmetry
slides.storyContext: Ravi draws three shapes on paper and challenges Meera: 'Can you find the lines of symmetry and say how many each shape has?' Meera takes a pencil and starts working.

example.problem: You have three letters: (A) Letter 'H', (B) Letter 'T', (C) Letter 'S'. For each, say: How many lines of symmetry does it have?
example.solution: (A) Letter 'H' has 2 lines of symmetry — one vertical through the middle and one horizontal through the middle. (B) Letter 'T' has 1 line of symmetry — a vertical line down the middle. (C) Letter 'S' has 0 lines of symmetry — it has rotational symmetry of order 2, but no fold line creates identical halves.

slides.inSimpleWords: Try folding or rotating shapes to see if they have lines of symmetry.

slides.title: Challenge: Design a Symmetric Rangoli
slides.storyContext: Dada challenges: 'Draw a simple geometric pattern in one quarter of a square, then mirror it to all four quarters using both horizontal and vertical symmetry.'

example.problem: Design a simple pattern (dots, lines, curves) in one quarter and mirror it 3 times to create a 4-fold symmetric design
example.solution: Create pattern in top-left. Mirror horizontally to top-right. Mirror both vertically to bottom-left and bottom-right. The result has both vertical and horizontal lines of symmetry.

slides.inSimpleWords: Mirroring in multiple directions creates complex, balanced patterns.

slides.title: Challenge: No Lines, But Rotational
slides.storyContext: Ravi asks: 'Can a shape have rotational symmetry but NO lines of symmetry?' Dada nods: 'Yes! The letter 'S' and the swastika are examples.'

example.problem: Find a shape with rotational symmetry order 2 but no line of symmetry
example.solution: The letter 'S' and the 'Z' both have 180° rotational symmetry but no lines of symmetry. Rotating them 180° shows they look the same, but no fold line creates matching halves.

slides.inSimpleWords: Some shapes spin symmetrically but don't fold symmetrically.

slides.title: Symmetry Summary
slides.storyContext: As the sun sets, Dada, Meera, and Ravi sit together. Dada says: 'Today you learned nature's secret to beauty: balance and order through symmetry.'

points.text: A line of symmetry divides a shape into two identical halves that match when folded.
Lines of symmetry can be vertical, horizontal, or diagonal.
Rotational symmetry means a shape looks the same after rotating it.
Different shapes have different numbers of lines of symmetry. A square has 4; a rectangle has 2.
Symmetry appears in nature (butterflies, leaves) and in design (rangoli, buildings, tiles).

slides.inSimpleWords: Symmetry creates balance. Look for lines where a shape matches itself when folded, or rotations where it looks identical.
